sections.h2: Does Vermont charge an estate tax, and who actually owes it?
sections.html:
Vermont charges an estate tax, but only on large estates. Under 32 V.S.A. § 7442a, an estate with a Vermont taxable estate under $5,000,000 owes nothing, and an estate of $5,000,000 or more owes 16 percent of the amount above $5,000,000.

The tax is figured on the whole estate, not on one house. A bank account, a retirement plan, a business interest and a Vermont home all count toward the total. An apportionment fraction then limits the tax to the Vermont share of the estate.

For most families who inherit a house in Vermont, the practical answer is that no Vermont estate tax is due. The Census Bureau reports a median value for owner-occupied homes in Vermont of $316,600 for 2020 to 2024. A single house at that level sits far below the $5 million line. Heirs of larger estates, or heirs who share a house with a big investment portfolio, are the people who need to look closer.

sections.html:

The federal exclusion is higher than the Vermont threshold, so an estate can owe Vermont estate tax while owing no federal estate tax.

sections.h2: When must an estate file a Vermont estate tax return?
sections.html:
An estate must file Form EST-191 when the person who died had an interest in Vermont property and the federal gross estate plus adjusted taxable gifts made within two years of death exceeds $5 million, or when a federal Form 706 is required. The Department of Taxes says the Legislature in 2026 raised the filing threshold to $5 million so that it matches the payment threshold.

Property located in Vermont for a resident does not include real or tangible property outside Vermont. For a nonresident, intangible property is also left out. A nonresident who owned a Vermont vacation house therefore counts the house, but not the brokerage account held in another state.

An executor also deals with other returns. The Department also lists an income tax return (IN-111) and a fiduciary return (FIT-161) if the estate earns income. If more time is needed for the estate tax return, Form EST-195 gives six months and must be filed on or before the due date.

sections.h2: Does Vermont have an inheritance tax on what heirs receive?
sections.html: The tax in Vermont is measured on the estate as a whole before anything is handed to heirs.

sections.h2: What federal rules affect an heir who sells a Vermont house?
sections.html:
The federal estate tax exclusion for people who die in 2026 is $15,000,000, according to the IRS, and a surviving spouse may elect to use the unused portion of the exclusion of the spouse who died.

The federal income tax on the sale is a different matter. The IRS explains in Topic 701 that the home sale exclusion of up to $250,000 of gain, or $500,000 on a joint return, depends on ownership and use tests of two years within five. An heir who never lived in the house usually does not meet those tests, so the gain on the sale is figured separately.

sections.h2: How does probate work when the estate owns a Vermont house?
sections.html:
When someone dies owning real estate in their own name, Vermont requires a formal estate, and the Probate Division of the Superior Court in the county where the person lived handles it. The Vermont Judiciary says a formal estate applies if the person owned real estate or the estate is worth more than $45,000.

The court recognizes an executor named in a will, or appoints an administrator if there is no will. Surviving spouses and next of kin have priority when suitable, and the personal representative generally posts a bond before appointment.

  • The inventory is due within 30 days of appointment, with assets valued at fair market value on the date of death.
  • The notice to creditors is published in a local newspaper within 30 days of appointment, and creditors then have four months from publication.
  • The personal representative should not pay claims until the four months pass.
  • If publication is skipped and unknown creditors exist, the claim window can stretch to three years after death.

These dates affect a sale because buyers and title companies want to see that debts and claims have been handled before they close.

sections.h2: Can the executor sell the house, and what paperwork records the sale?
sections.html:
Yes, but a personal representative who wants to sell, convey, mortgage or lease real estate files a motion for a license with the court. The Judiciary names the Motion for License to Sell or Convey Real Estate (form 700-00035) and a report on the license afterward.

One Vermont title resource describes the next steps this way: after the sale the personal representative signs the deed before an authorized officer and records it with the town or city clerk where the property sits, and the deed refers to the license order. When the debts and expenses are paid, the court issues a decree of distribution, and a certified copy is recorded in the town land records so that title is clear for the heirs.

Vermont land records are kept by town clerks, not by a single county office. Recording a document costs $15.00 per page under 32 V.S.A. § 1671(a)(6), and a property transfer tax return costs a flat $15.00 to record, according to a town fee schedule published in 2025. Your town clerk can confirm the current amounts.

sections.h2: What is the Vermont property transfer tax when an estate sells?
sections.html:
A sale out of an estate to a buyer is a transfer by deed, so the Vermont property transfer tax applies unless an exemption fits. The tax is due within 30 days of the closing date, according to the Department of Taxes.

  • Buyer's principal residence: 0.5 percent on the first $200,000 of value, then 1.25 percent above that, plus a 0.22 percent Clean Water Surcharge on the amount above $200,000.
  • Year-round home that is not a principal residence and not a long-term rental: 3.40 percent, or 3.62 percent with the surcharge.
  • Property not fit for year-round habitation: 1.25 percent plus the 0.22 percent surcharge.

The exemption list in 32 V.S.A. § 9603 that we read includes transfers without actual consideration between spouses, parent and child, or grandparent and grandchild, and it has no separate line for transfers by will or intestacy.

sections.h2: What if the heir or the estate is not a Vermont resident?
sections.html:
When the seller is a nonresident, the buyer must withhold 2.5 percent of the sale price and send it to the Department of Taxes, unless the seller has a Commissioner's Certificate. The buyer files Form RW-171 with payment within 30 days of the transfer, and the seller claims the amount as a credit on Form IN-111.

A seller can ask for a Commissioner's Certificate through myVTax to reduce or remove withholding. The seller must be in good standing, with all required Vermont returns filed and taxes paid, and must document the property's basis. For an inherited house the Department lists examples such as an estate inventory. Heirs who live out of state should start this step early so the closing is not held up.

sections.h2: What does a seller of an inherited Vermont house also need to disclose or pay?
sections.html:
A seller must give the buyer flood information before or as part of the contract. Under 27 V.S.A. § 380, the seller provides a copy or link to the FEMA flood insurance rate map, says whether the property flooded or suffered flood damage while the seller possessed it, and says whether flood insurance is carried or required. If the seller fails to do this, the buyer can terminate before title or occupancy transfers and can sue for damages and attorney's fees.

Property tax is the other running cost. Vermont education property tax rates differ for homestead and nonhomestead property, and a house that is not declared a homestead is taxed as nonhomestead. A house that no owner lives in as a domicile on April 1 generally falls on the nonhomestead side, so ask the town how an estate-held house is classified.

sections.h2: How does Vermont's size and layout shape an estate sale?
sections.html: Vermont has 14 counties and 247 municipalities, so an estate sale touches a county probate court and a town clerk that may be in different places. Chittenden County, with Burlington, is the most populous at 168,323 residents in the 2020 Census, and Essex County is the smallest at 5,920.

faqs.q: At what value does Vermont tax an estate?
faqs.a: Vermont taxes an estate only when the Vermont taxable estate reaches $5,000,000. The rate is 16 percent of the amount above $5,000,000, adjusted by an apportionment fraction.

faqs.q: Does an heir pay tax just for inheriting a Vermont house?
faqs.a: No Vermont tax on the act of inheriting appears on the Department of Taxes estate tax page. The estate tax is paid by the estate. Selling the house can still create transfer tax, income tax or withholding questions.

faqs.q: Do I need probate before I sell an inherited house in Vermont?
faqs.a: Usually yes, if the house was in the decedent's own name. The Vermont Judiciary says a formal estate applies when the person owned real estate. The personal representative may need court permission, called a license, to sell.

faqs.q: How long does an executor have to file the inventory?
faqs.a: The inventory is due within 30 days of appointment, per the Vermont Judiciary, with assets valued at fair market value on the date of death.

faqs.q: What is the Vermont withholding rate on a nonresident seller?
faqs.a: The buyer withholds 2.5 percent of the sale price on Form RW-171 unless the seller holds a Commissioner's Certificate. The buyer files within 30 days of the transfer.
